name: Quadratic formula (x₁)
description: Returns one root x₁ of the quadratic equation ax²+bx+c=0 using (−b+√(b²−4ac))/(2a). This is the root taking the plus sign of the square root.
notes: Requires a≠0. If the discriminant b²−4ac is negative the roots are complex and this real formula does not apply.

name: Percentage (part ÷ whole)
description: Expresses the part as a percentage of the whole, computing part÷whole×100. The result tells you what share of the total the part represents.
notes: The whole must be nonzero. Result is a percentage, so 0.5 as a fraction here would be entered as part and whole values, not as 50.

name: Power (base^exp)
description: Raises base to the power of exponent, computing base^exponent. The exponent may be negative or fractional, giving reciprocals or roots respectively.
notes: A negative base with a fractional exponent may be undefined for real numbers. A zero base with a negative exponent is undefined (division by zero).

name: Logarithm (log_base x)
description: Computes the logarithm of x in an arbitrary base, using ln(x)÷ln(base). The result is the exponent to which the base must be raised to obtain x.
notes: Requires x>0, base>0 and base≠1. The default base is 10 (common logarithm); set base to e for the natural logarithm.

name: Quadratic formula (x₂)
description: Computes one root of the quadratic equation a x squared plus b x plus c equals zero using the minus branch of the quadratic formula: negative b minus the square root of the discriminant, all over two a. The result is that root x2.
notes: If the discriminant b squared minus 4ac is negative the root is not real, and a must be nonzero. This branch gives one of two roots; the plus branch gives the other.

name: Discriminant
description: Calculates the discriminant of a quadratic equation, b squared minus four times a times c. Its sign tells how many real roots the equation has: positive gives two, zero gives one, and negative gives none.
notes: A zero discriminant means a repeated (double) real root; a negative value means the two roots are complex conjugates. The coefficient a must be nonzero for a quadratic.

name: Arithmetic sequence (nth term)
description: Gives the nth term of an arithmetic sequence by adding (n minus 1) common differences d to the first term a1. The result is the value of the term at position n.
notes: The term index n should be a positive integer, and the common difference d is the fixed step added between consecutive terms; a negative d makes the sequence decrease.

name: Arithmetic series (sum)
description: Computes the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence with first term a1 and common difference d, as n over two times the quantity two a1 plus (n minus 1) d. The result is the running total of those terms.
notes: The number of terms n should be a positive integer. Equivalently this is n times the average of the first and last terms; a negative d can make the sum decrease.

name: Geometric sequence (nth term)
description: Computes the nth term of a geometric sequence, where each term is the previous one multiplied by the common ratio r. Starting from the first term a1, it returns a1 times r raised to the power (n minus 1).
notes: Term numbering starts at 1, so the first term uses n=1 and gives a1 (r to the power 0). A ratio between 0 and 1 shrinks the terms, while a negative r makes them alternate in sign.

name: Geometric series (sum)
description: Computes the sum of the first n terms of a geometric series with first term a1 and common ratio r, using a1×(1−r^n)/(1−r). It totals a1 + a1·r + a1·r² and so on up to n terms.
notes: This formula requires r not equal to 1; if r equals 1 the sum is simply a1×n. The exponent n is the number of terms, not the last term index.

name: Infinite geometric series (sum)
description: Computes the sum of an infinite geometric series a1 + a1·r + a1·r² + … as a1/(1−r). The infinitely many terms converge to this finite value when the ratio is small enough in magnitude.
notes: The series converges only when the absolute value of r is less than 1; otherwise the sum does not exist. As r approaches 1 the total grows without bound.

name: Compound interest
description: Computes the final amount when principal p earns interest at annual rate r, compounded n times per year for t years, using p×(1 + r/n)^(n·t). More frequent compounding yields a slightly larger amount.
notes: Enter the rate as a decimal, so 5 percent is 0.05, not 5. The result is the total value including principal, not just the interest earned.

name: Continuous compound interest
description: Computes the final amount when principal p is compounded continuously at annual rate r for t years, using p×e^(r·t). This is the limiting case of compounding infinitely often.
notes: Enter the rate as a decimal (5 percent is 0.05). The continuous result is slightly higher than any finite compounding frequency at the same nominal rate.

name: Exponential growth
description: Computes a quantity growing exponentially at constant rate r per period, using a×(1 + r)^t from an initial value a over time t. Each period multiplies the value by the factor (1 + r).
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period, so 3 percent is 0.03. Time t and the rate must use the same period; a negative r would instead represent decay.

name: Exponential decay
description: Computes the amount remaining after exponential decay, using a×e^(−k·t) from initial amount a with decay constant k over time t. Larger k or longer t leaves less of the substance.
notes: The decay constant k relates to half-life by k = ln(2)/half-life; make sure k and t use the same time unit. The result approaches but never reaches zero.

name: Half-life remaining amount
description: Computes how much of an initial amount a remains after elapsed time t, given a half-life h, using a×0.5^(t/h). The quantity halves once for every interval of length h that passes.
notes: The elapsed time t and half-life h must share the same time unit. After one half-life half remains, after two a quarter, and so on.

name: Doubling time
description: Computes how long it takes for a quantity to double when growing at a constant per-period rate r, using ln(2)/ln(1 + r). The result is expressed in the same periods used for the rate.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period, so 7 percent is 0.07. This is the exact formula; the Rule of 72 is only an approximation of it.

name: Present value
description: Computes the value today of a future amount fv received after n periods, discounted at rate r per period, using fv/(1 + r)^n. It answers how much a future sum is worth now.
notes: Enter r as a decimal per period, and use the same period for r and n. A higher discount rate or more periods gives a smaller present value.

name: Simple interest total
description: Computes the total amount when principal p earns simple interest at annual rate r for t years, using p×(1 + r·t). Interest is charged only on the original principal, not on accumulated interest.
notes: Enter r as a decimal (5 percent is 0.05) and t in years. Unlike compound interest, the interest each year stays constant at p×r.

name: Law of cosines (side c)
description: Computes the length of the third side c of a triangle from two sides a and b and the angle γ between them, using sqrt(a² + b² − 2ab·cos γ). It generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to non-right triangles.
notes: The angle γ must be entered in radians and must be the angle opposite side c, that is between sides a and b. When γ is a right angle the formula reduces to a² + b².

name: Law of cosines (angle)
description: Computes the interior angle opposite side c of a triangle from the three side lengths a, b, c, using acos((a² + b² − c²)/(2ab)). It recovers an angle when all three sides are known.
notes: The result is in radians and gives the angle facing side c. The three lengths must form a valid triangle, otherwise the argument falls outside acos's domain.

name: Law of sines (side a)
description: Computes an unknown side a of a triangle from a known side b and the two opposite angles, using b×sin α/sin β, where α faces a and β faces b. It applies the law of sines to solve for a side.
notes: Both angles must be in radians, with α opposite the unknown side a and β opposite the known side b. The angle β must not be zero.

name: Triangle area (two sides & angle)
description: Computes the area of a triangle from two sides a and b and the included angle γ between them, using 0.5×a×b×sin γ. It is handy when the height is not directly known.
notes: The angle γ must be in radians and must be the angle between the two given sides. The area is largest when γ is a right angle.

name: Heron's formula
description: Computes the area of a triangle from only its three side lengths a, b, c. It forms the semi-perimeter s = (a+b+c)/2, then takes sqrt(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)).
notes: The three lengths must satisfy the triangle inequality, or the value under the square root becomes negative. No angles or height are needed.

name: Distance between two points
description: Computes the straight-line distance between two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) in a plane, using sqrt((x2−x1)² + (y2−y1)²). It is the Pythagorean theorem applied to coordinate differences.
notes: This is the Euclidean distance in two dimensions; both points must use the same coordinate units. The result is always non-negative and independent of point order.

name: Midpoint (x-coordinate)
description: Computes the x-coordinate of the midpoint between two points with x-coordinates x1 and x2, as their average (x1 + x2)/2. It gives the point halfway along the x-axis.
notes: This handles only the x-component; the y-coordinate of the midpoint is found the same way from y1 and y2. The result lies exactly between the two inputs.

name: Linear interpolation
description: Estimates the y-value at a query point x on the straight line through two known points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), using y1 + (x−x1)(y2−y1)/(x2−x1). It reads a value linearly between two data points.
notes: The two x-values must differ so the slope is defined. Choosing an x outside the range from x1 to x2 extrapolates rather than interpolates.

name: Percent error
description: Computes the percent error of a measured value o relative to the actual value a, using abs((o−a)/a)×100. It expresses the size of the discrepancy as a percentage of the true value.
notes: The absolute value makes the result non-negative regardless of whether the measurement is high or low. It is undefined when the actual value a is zero.

name: Percent change
description: Computes the percentage change from an initial value a to a final value b, using (b−a)/a×100. A positive result means an increase and a negative result means a decrease.
notes: The change is measured relative to the initial value a, which must not be zero. Unlike percent error, the sign is kept to show direction.

name: Weighted mean (two values)
description: Computes the weighted average of two values x1 and x2 with weights w1 and w2, using (w1·x1 + w2·x2)/(w1 + w2). Values with larger weights pull the average toward themselves.
notes: The weights need not sum to 1 because the formula divides by their total. If both weights are equal this reduces to the ordinary arithmetic mean.

name: Arithmetic mean (two values)
description: Computes the arithmetic mean of two values a and b as their sum divided by two, (a + b)/2. It is the ordinary average and lies exactly halfway between the two values.
notes: The result always falls between the two inputs. For quantities like rates or ratios, the geometric or harmonic mean may be more appropriate.

name: Geometric mean (two values)
description: Computes the geometric mean of two values a and b as sqrt(a·b). It is the central tendency suited to multiplicative quantities such as growth rates or ratios.
notes: Both values should be positive for a real result, since a negative product has no real square root. The geometric mean never exceeds the arithmetic mean.

name: Harmonic mean (two values)
description: Computes the harmonic mean of two values a and b as 2ab/(a + b). It is the appropriate average for rates such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: Both values should be positive and nonzero. The harmonic mean is always the smallest of the three classic means, at or below the geometric and arithmetic means.

name: pH from concentration
description: Computes the pH of a solution from its hydrogen ion concentration [H⁺] in mol/L, using −log10([H⁺]). Lower pH means a more acidic, higher-concentration solution.
notes: The log here is base 10, and the concentration must be in mol/L and greater than zero. A pH of 7 is neutral, below 7 acidic, and above 7 basic at 25 degrees C.

name: Decibel level
description: Computes a power ratio expressed in decibels, using 10×log10(p/p0), where p is the measured intensity and p0 a reference. It converts a multiplicative ratio into a logarithmic scale.
notes: This 10×log form is for power or intensity ratios; amplitude ratios use 20×log instead. Every 10 dB corresponds to a tenfold change in power.

name: Change base to natural log ratio
description: Computes the base-2 logarithm of x via the change-of-base formula ln(x)/ln(2). The result is the power to which 2 must be raised to obtain x.
notes: The input x must be positive. The same pattern, dividing ln(x) by ln(base), converts a natural log into a logarithm of any other base.

name: Angle of a slope
description: Computes the inclination angle of the line between two points, using atan((y2−y1)/(x2−x1)). It returns the angle the slope makes with the horizontal.
notes: The result is in radians and the x-values must differ to avoid division by zero. Because it uses a single-argument arctangent, the angle is limited to between −pi/2 and pi/2.

name: Sum of first n integers
description: Computes the sum of the first n positive integers, 1 + 2 + ... + n, using the closed form n*(n+1)/2. It gives the total directly without adding the terms one by one.
notes: n should be a positive integer. The product n*(n+1) is always even, so the result is a whole number. These sums are the triangular numbers.

name: Sum of first n squares
description: Computes the sum of the first n squares, 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2, using the closed form n*(n+1)*(2*n+1)/6. It gives the total directly from n alone.
notes: n should be a positive integer. The product n*(n+1)*(2*n+1) is always divisible by 6, so the result is a whole number. These are the square pyramidal numbers.

name: Sum of first n cubes
description: Computes the sum of the first n cubes, 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3, using the closed form (n*(n+1)/2)^2. Notably this equals the square of the sum of the first n integers.
notes: n should be a positive integer. The result is always a perfect square, since it is the square of the nth triangular number n*(n+1)/2.

name: Sum of first n odd numbers
description: Computes the sum of the first n odd numbers, 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n-1), which equals exactly n^2. Adding consecutive odd numbers always produces a perfect square.
notes: n should be a positive integer and counts how many odd numbers are summed, not the largest odd number. The result n^2 is always a perfect square.

name: nth pentagonal number
description: Computes the nth pentagonal number using n*(3*n-1)/2. Pentagonal numbers count dots arranged in nested pentagonal patterns, giving the sequence 1, 5, 12, 22, 35, and so on.
notes: n should be a positive integer indexing the sequence. The product n*(3*n-1) is always even, so the result is a whole number. This gives the standard (not generalized) pentagonal numbers.

name: nth hexagonal number
description: Computes the nth hexagonal number using n*(2*n-1). Hexagonal numbers count dots arranged in nested hexagonal patterns, giving the sequence 1, 6, 15, 28, 45, and so on.
notes: n should be a positive integer indexing the sequence. Every hexagonal number is also a triangular number. The result is always a whole number.

name: nth Fibonacci number (Binet)
description: Computes the n-th Fibonacci number directly with Binet's closed-form formula, using the golden ratio phi=(1+sqrt(5))/2 and its conjugate. The result is rounded to the nearest integer, giving the term in the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ... without iterating.
notes: n is a non-negative integer index. Floating-point rounding errors make the result unreliable for large n (roughly n above 70), where an exact integer method is preferable.

name: Permutations nP2
description: Counts the number of ordered arrangements of 2 items chosen from n distinct items, equal to n*(n-1). Order matters, so picking A then B differs from B then A.
notes: n must be an integer of at least 2; otherwise the count is not meaningful. Items are assumed distinct and selected without replacement.

name: Permutations nP3
description: Counts the number of ordered arrangements of 3 items chosen from n distinct items, equal to n*(n-1)*(n-2). Each different order of the same three items is counted separately.
notes: n must be an integer of at least 3. Items are distinct and chosen without replacement; order is significant.

name: Combinations nC2
description: Counts the number of unordered pairs that can be chosen from n distinct items, equal to n*(n-1)/2. Unlike permutations, order does not matter, so pair A-B is the same as B-A.
notes: n must be an integer of at least 2. Items are distinct and selected without replacement; the result is always a whole number.

name: Combinations nC3
description: Counts the number of unordered triples that can be chosen from n distinct items, equal to n*(n-1)*(n-2)/6. Order within a group of three is ignored.
notes: n must be an integer of at least 3. Items are distinct and chosen without replacement; the division by 6 removes the 3! orderings of each triple.

name: Polar to rectangular x
description: Converts polar coordinates to the x (horizontal) Cartesian coordinate using x = r*cos(theta), where r is the radius and theta the angle. This gives the point's projection onto the horizontal axis.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. A negative r reflects the point through the origin; theta is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis.

name: Polar to rectangular y
description: Converts polar coordinates to the y (vertical) Cartesian coordinate using y = r*sin(theta), where r is the radius and theta the angle. This gives the point's projection onto the vertical axis.
notes: The angle theta must be in radians. theta is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis; pair this with x = r*cos(theta) for the full point.

name: Rectangular to polar angle
description: Computes the polar angle of a point (x, y) as atan(y/x), the direction from the origin measured in radians. It represents the angle the line to the point makes with the positive x-axis.
notes: Single-argument atan returns values only in the range -pi/2 to pi/2, so it cannot distinguish the left half-plane; add pi when x is negative. Undefined when x is zero.

name: Distance on number line
description: Computes the distance between two points a and b on a number line as the absolute value of their difference, |b - a|. The result is a non-negative length independent of which point is larger.
notes: Because the absolute value is taken, the order of a and b does not affect the result. This is the one-dimensional case of Euclidean distance.

name: Midpoint
description: Computes the midpoint of two values a and b on a number line as their average, (a + b)/2. The result is the point exactly halfway between them.
notes: This is the one-dimensional midpoint; for points in a plane apply the same average separately to each coordinate. Works with negative values.

name: Slope-intercept line y
description: Evaluates a straight line in slope-intercept form, y = m*x + b, giving the y value at a given x. Here m is the slope (rise over run) and b is the y-intercept where the line crosses the y-axis.
notes: The slope m and intercept b define the whole line; this returns only the y value for one chosen x. A slope of zero gives a horizontal line at height b.

name: Relative error
description: Computes the relative error of a measured value against the true value as |measured - actual| / |actual|. It expresses the size of the error as a fraction of the true magnitude.
notes: The result is a fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Undefined when the actual value is zero, and it can be misleading for true values very close to zero.

name: Logarithm power rule (base 10)
description: Applies the logarithm power rule in base 10: log(x^p) = p*log(x). It computes the base-10 logarithm of x raised to the power p by multiplying log(x) by the exponent p.
notes: The argument x must be positive. The exponent p may be any real number; log here denotes the base-10 logarithm, not the natural log.

name: Logarithm product rule (base 10)
description: Applies the logarithm product rule in base 10: log(a*b) = log(a) + log(b). It computes the base-10 logarithm of the product a*b as the sum of the individual logarithms.
notes: Both a and b must be positive for the logarithms to be defined. log denotes the base-10 logarithm; the identity holds for any logarithm base.

name: Half-life amount
description: Computes the remaining amount after exponential decay by half-life, a0*(1/2)^(t/h), where a0 is the initial amount, t the elapsed time and h the half-life. The quantity halves each time t increases by one half-life.
notes: Time t and half-life h must use the same time unit. The result carries the same unit as a0; over one half-life the amount drops to exactly half.

name: Continuous growth
description: Computes the value of a quantity under continuous exponential growth, p*exp(r*t), where p is the principal or initial amount, r the continuous rate and t the time. It gives the amount after continuous compounding.
notes: The rate r is a decimal per unit time (0.05 means 5 percent), and r and t must share the same time unit. A negative r models continuous decay.

name: Sine angle-sum
description: Evaluates the sine angle-sum identity, sin(a+b) = sin(a)cos(b) + cos(a)sin(b), returning the sine of the combined angle a+b from the sines and cosines of the individual angles.
notes: Angles a and b must be in radians. The output equals sin(a+b) and therefore always lies between -1 and 1.

name: Cosine angle-sum
description: Evaluates the cosine angle-sum identity, cos(a+b) = cos(a)cos(b) - sin(a)sin(b), returning the cosine of the combined angle a+b from the sines and cosines of the individual angles.
notes: Angles a and b must be in radians. Note the minus sign, which distinguishes this from the sine sum identity; the output always lies between -1 and 1.

name: Hyperbolic sine (sinh)
description: Computes the hyperbolic sine of x, defined as (exp(x) - exp(-x))/2. Unlike ordinary sine it is unbounded, growing roughly like exp(x)/2 for large positive x and it is an odd function.
notes: x is a plain real number, not an angle in the trigonometric sense. sinh is odd, so sinh(-x) = -sinh(x), and sinh(0) = 0.

name: Hyperbolic cosine (cosh)
description: Computes the hyperbolic cosine of x, defined as (exp(x) + exp(-x))/2. It is an even function with a minimum value of 1 at x=0 and describes the shape of a hanging chain (catenary).
notes: x is a plain real number, not a trigonometric angle. cosh is always at least 1, and cosh(-x) = cosh(x).

name: Hyperbolic tangent (tanh)
description: Computes the hyperbolic tangent of x, the ratio sinh(x)/cosh(x) written as (exp(x) - exp(-x))/(exp(x) + exp(-x)). It is an odd, S-shaped function that smoothly approaches -1 and +1 as x goes to negative and positive infinity.
notes: x is a plain real number. The output always lies strictly between -1 and 1; tanh is widely used as a saturating activation function.

name: Weighted mean (3 values)
description: Computes the weighted mean of three values x1, x2, x3 with weights w1, w2, w3 as (w1*x1 + w2*x2 + w3*x3)/(w1 + w2 + w3). Larger weights pull the average toward their associated values.
notes: The sum of the weights must not be zero. Weights need not add up to 1; the denominator normalizes them automatically.

name: Harmonic mean (3 values)
description: Computes the harmonic mean of three values a, b, c as 3 divided by the sum of their reciprocals, 3/(1/a + 1/b + 1/c). It is the appropriate average for rates such as speeds over equal distances.
notes: None of a, b, c may be zero, and typically all are positive. The harmonic mean is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean.

name: Geometric mean (3 values)
description: Computes the geometric mean of three values a, b, c as the cube root of their product, cbrt(a*b*c). It is the central tendency suited to quantities that combine multiplicatively, such as growth rates.
notes: Values should be positive for the mean to be meaningful. The geometric mean never exceeds the arithmetic mean of the same values.

name: Law of tangents ratio
description: Evaluates the ratio in the law of tangents, tan((a-b)/2)/tan((a+b)/2), for two angles a and b of a triangle. This equals the ratio of the differences to the sums of the opposite side lengths.
notes: Angles a and b must be in radians. The sum a+b must be less than pi (a valid triangle), and tan((a+b)/2) must not be zero.

name: Slope between two points
description: Computes the slope of the line through two points (x1, y1) and (x2, y2) as the rise over the run, (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1). It measures how steeply y changes with x.
notes: Undefined when x1 equals x2, which corresponds to a vertical line. A positive slope rises left to right, a negative one falls.

name: Cotangent
description: Computes the cotangent of an angle x as cos(x)/sin(x), the reciprocal of the tangent. It gives the ratio of the adjacent side to the opposite side in a right triangle.
notes: The angle x must be in radians. Undefined wherever sin(x) is zero, that is at integer multiples of pi.

name: Secant
description: Computes the secant of an angle x as 1/cos(x), the reciprocal of the cosine. It gives the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side in a right triangle.
notes: The angle x must be in radians. Undefined wherever cos(x) is zero, that is at pi/2 plus integer multiples of pi; the magnitude is always at least 1.

name: Double-angle sine
description: Evaluates the double-angle identity for sine, sin(2x) = 2*sin(x)*cos(x). It returns the sine of twice the angle x using only the sine and cosine of x.
notes: The angle x must be in radians. The output equals sin(2x) and therefore always lies between -1 and 1.

name: Double-angle cosine
description: Evaluates the double-angle identity for cosine, cos(2x) = cos(x)^2 - sin(x)^2. It returns the cosine of twice the angle x from the squared cosine and sine of x.
notes: The angle x must be in radians. Equivalent forms are 2cos(x)^2 - 1 and 1 - 2sin(x)^2; the output always lies between -1 and 1.

name: Geometric series sum
description: Computes the sum of the first n terms of a geometric series with first term a and common ratio r, using a*(1 - r^n)/(1 - r). Each term is r times the previous one.
notes: This form requires r not equal to 1; if r equals 1 the sum is simply a*n. n is the number of terms and should be a positive integer.

name: Degrees to radians
description: Converts an angle from degrees to radians using d*pi/180. Radians express angle as arc length per unit radius, the standard unit for trigonometric functions.
notes: The input d is in degrees and the output in radians. A full turn of 360 degrees equals 2*pi radians.

name: Radians to degrees
description: Converts an angle from radians to degrees using r*180/pi. This is the inverse of the degrees-to-radians conversion and expresses the angle in the familiar 360-degree scale.
notes: The input r is in radians and the output in degrees. pi radians corresponds to 180 degrees.
